questions.prompt: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights?

options.text: It finalises a vertex assuming no shorter path exists, which a later negative edge can violate
It cannot handle more than one source

questions.explanation: Dijkstra greedily locks in the closest vertex, but a negative edge encountered later could have produced a cheaper path, breaking that assumption. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights instead.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary heap on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: Each vertex extraction and each edge relaxation costs O(log V) with a binary heap, giving O((V + E) log V). A Fibonacci heap improves this to O(E + V log V).

questions.prompt: Bellman-Ford finds single-source shortest paths and can also:

options.text: Find the longest path in any graph
Detect the presence of a negative-weight cycle

questions.explanation: After V-1 relaxation passes distances should be final; if a V-th pass still relaxes an edge, a negative cycle is reachable. This detection is something Dijkstra cannot do.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
questions.explanation: It relaxes all E edges across V-1 passes, giving O(V x E). This is slower than Dijkstra but is the price of handling negative weights.

options.text: Shortest paths between all pairs of vertices

questions.explanation: It uses dynamic programming over intermediate vertices to fill an all-pairs distance matrix in O(V^3). It is convenient for dense graphs and tolerates negative edges without negative cycles.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm processes edges by:

options.text: Increasing weight, adding an edge if it does not form a cycle
The order they appear in the input
Decreasing weight, always adding the heaviest edge

questions.explanation: Sorting edges ascending and adding each unless it connects two already-joined components builds a minimum spanning tree. A union-find structure performs the cycle test efficiently.

questions.prompt: Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm grows the tree by:

options.text: Removing the heaviest edges from the graph
Adding all edges of the lightest vertex
Repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that connects a new vertex to the tree
Sorting all edges once and adding them in order

questions.explanation: Prim's expands a single tree, each step pulling in the minimum-weight edge crossing to a new vertex, using a priority queue. Kruskal's, by contrast, may grow several fragments at once.

questions.prompt: If every edge in a connected graph has a distinct weight, its minimum spanning tree is:

options.text: Unique only if the graph is a tree

questions.explanation: Distinct weights remove the ties that allow alternative trees, so the MST is unique. With repeated weights, several minimum spanning trees of equal total weight can exist.

questions.prompt: For a directed acyclic graph, single-source shortest paths can be found in O(V + E) by:

options.text: Running Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap

questions.explanation: Because a DAG has no cycles, processing vertices in topological order guarantees each is finalised before its successors, needing just one linear pass. This even works with negative weights.

questions.prompt: The minimum weight edge crossing any cut of a graph is:

options.text: Never in a minimum spanning tree
Always in some minimum spanning tree (the cut property)
Only in the MST if it is the global minimum edge

questions.explanation: The cut property states that the lightest edge crossing any partition of the vertices belongs to a minimum spanning tree. It is the theoretical foundation of both Prim's and Kruskal's correctness.
